title: Todd Blanche, Trump's ex-lawyer, narrowly confirmed as attorney general
description: US President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche has been narrowly confirmed as attorney general - the nation's top law enforcement off
body: US President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche has been narrowly confirmed as attorney general - the nation's top law enforcement official.The vote brings to an end a lengthy standoff between Senate Republicans and the Trump administration over Blanche, who has served as acting attorney general since April.Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote overnight, with two Republican senators, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, joining all Democrats to oppose his nomination.Senator Bill Cassidy cast the deciding vote, a decision closely watched in Washington given the years of acrimony between the Louisiana Republican and Trump.After the vote, Blanche said he was "deeply honoured by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me".Some Republican senators had raised concerns about Blache's handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents and his role in establishing Trump's $1.8bn (£1.3bn) "anti-weaponisation" fund.The fund was planned to provide compensation to individuals who alleged government persecution but critics including Murkowski feared it would go to individuals who were prosecuted for participating in the 6 January attack on Congress in 2021.Blanche eventually pledged to walk back the fund after blowback from Republican senators during his confirmation hearings.It remains unclear whether the commitment is legally binding or whether Trump could later persuade Blanche, his former personal attorney, to revive a similar scheme under another name.The issues surrounding Blanche meant Senators Collins and Murkowski held off from backing Blanche, with the latter citing her lack of confidence in Blanche to "check the worst impulses of this administration".Murkowski announced on Friday she would oppose Blanche, citing concerns over the "politicisation" of the justice department.Collins also raised concerns about Blanche's role in settling Trump's $10bn lawsuit with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), but said he ultimately trusted Blanche to give the president ​candid legal advice.Before casting the deciding vote, Cassidy announced that he believed Blanche was the best option the president would put forward."This is not a referendum on President Trump, it is a decision regarding Mr Blanche, in very specific circumstances," said Cassidy on Friday. "All considered, I will vote for Mr Blanche."Cassidy acknowledged Trump is the ultimate decider on the direction of the justice department, but that Senate confirmation would give Blanche "greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for."During Trump's second impeachment in 2021, Cassidy voted to convict Trump over the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot. The vote did not pass, and when Trump returned to office, he successfully forced Cassidy into retirement by backing a primary challenger for his Louisiana Senate seat earlier this year.In a post on X, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer expressed concern that Blanche's appointment would be an "excuse on a silver platter to keep up his pervasive, breathtaking corruption"."Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump's corruption. He advanced his career enabling it," he wrote. "Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too."But most Republicans swiftly celebrated the victory. Iowa Republican Senator Chuck Grassley - chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee - wrote on X that Blanche had shown "extraordinary patience, compassion [and] tenacity" throughout the appointment process. "There's no doubt he's qualified," Grassley wrote. Blanche was already deputy attorney general when he took up the interim leadership role in April, after Pam Bondi was fired.

schema.headline: Todd Blanche, Trump's ex-lawyer, narrowly confirmed as attorney general

title: Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
description: Figure caption, Watch footage from a Levy sexual assault victim that was passed to policeByAdam GoldsmithPolice have urged more victims of Simon Levy
body: Figure caption, Watch footage from a Levy sexual assault victim that was passed to policeByAdam GoldsmithPolice have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks. The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday. The Met, British Transport Police (BTP) and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) have all admitted failures in how Levy was monitored between his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges and his arrest for murder in September 2025.On Saturday, Simons told BBC Breakfast a "multi-agency review" was needed, saying: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."Simons said public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".The Met said its detectives had "exhausted numerous lines of enquiry - including working with coroners – to identify whether Levy is responsible for any similar, unsolved incidents, including deaths".No further victims have been identified so far but the force urged "anyone who believes they may be a victim of his to contact police".Levy is known to have attacked at least 10 women on public transport in London, seeking out busy carriages to assault passengers.BTP said more women "may recognise [Levy] and have not yet reported what has happened to them".Image source, Met PoliceImage caption, Levy was found guilty of murdering Sheryl Wilkins (l), 39, and Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he committed a violent rape in January 2025.He went on to kill Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March of that year and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months later.Earlier this year he was found guilty by a jury at Inner London Crown Court of groping 10 women on the Tube and an 11th while in prison, but details of that case could only be reported this week at the conclusion of his murder trial.The offence in the prison took place on April 2022. The Tube assaults then occurred between 24 October 2023 and May 2025.He had already been convicted of sexually assaulting two women in 2018, which he was jailed for in 2021.BTP has confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect." Lisa Squire, whose daughter Libby was murdered by a man who had previously committed a string of sex crimes, told the BBC that a "catalogue of disasters" had led to Levy's murders.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme "the patterns were there, he was flying those red flags", and said there were "precursor offences" for which he could have stopped by police."At the moment, the message going out, in my opinion, is that women's safety is not important," she continued.Zoë Billingham, a former independent police inspector who pushed for reforms on how violence against women in girls is policed, said that "too often in cases like this the dots aren't being joined up".She added: "It's not one or two missed opportunities that could have brought him to justice, that could have had him locked up and behind bars and no longer a threat to women and girls. It was an extraordinary succession."

schema.headline: Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'

title: Daniel Kinahan: Irish government jet travels to UAE for extradition
description: The Irish government jet has travelled to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as part of an operation to extradite suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan.Kina
body: The Irish government jet has travelled to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as part of an operation to extradite suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan.Kinahan was arrested in Dubai under a warrant issued by the Irish courts in April but has fought attempts to extradite him.His appeals have been unsuccessful and it is expected that he is due to be flown back to Ireland on Sunday, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ.He will then be taken to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin.On Kinhan's return to Ireland, RTÉ have said that a large security operation will be in place and the prison service has also upgraded facilities in the maximum-security Portlaoise Prison.The US government imposed sanctions on him in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.An extradition agreement is in place between the UAE and Ireland and it was used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the organised crime group.He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.For more than 20 years the group has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world, the National Crime Agency (NCA) previously said.The NCA said the crime group is linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.The US Treasury Department describes the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world, comparable to crime organisations like Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza.A reward of up to $5m (£3.84m) has also been offered by the US for information on the three most senior Kinahan gang members - Daniel, his father Christopher Snr, 65, and brother Christopher Jnr.According to former Gardaí (Irish police) Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£836,590,000) globally from its activities.In 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively.The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m.Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Irish government jet travels to UAE for extradition

title: Full body MOTs - the future of healthcare or a headache for the NHS?
description: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shockImage source, BBC and Neko HealthImage caption, More than 2,000 images were taken of Ruth's
body: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shockImage source, BBC and Neko HealthImage caption, More than 2,000 images were taken of Ruth's skinByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporter I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital. While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest £299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.Image caption, The body scan industry sees this kind of treatment as a new frontier in healthcareI will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders. I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients. My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it."While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.'My cancerous skin marks were missed'Image source, AnnabelImage caption, Annabel had four cancerous markings removedAnnabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology."I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions."It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment."Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment."We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".'It saved my life'Image source, MehvishImage caption, Mehvish's long-term blood sugar levels came back very high and she was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune DiabetesMehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis."I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2. Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise."I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one."I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden."But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.Image source, NEKOImage caption, One of the moles that were flagged as needing extra scrutiny by dermatologists in SwedenHaving felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS. Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal Society of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan. But former health minister Steve Brine, who acts as an advisor to a preventative healthcare company, says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health"."Change is afoot across the NHS - prevention is a huge policy area," Brine says. "We want to identify people's problems before they become patients, so these scans could well become a part of our future healthcare and primary care needs to adapt."As for me? I was told my heart age was four years younger than my actual age, and on the whole, I was in tip-top health. But I've also learned a valuable lesson - that I could be more at risk of skin cancer because of my freckles. So, thanks to my time in the scanner, I am now far more enthusiastic about lathering sunscreen all over my body - rather than only on my face.

schema.headline: Full body MOTs - the future of healthcare or a headache for the NHS?

title: Are the 'luteal uglies' a real thing?
description: "Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their
body: "Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their luteal phase."The video has 2.4 million views and hundreds of comments."This is literally me," one woman writes. "I'm angry at how accurate this is," another says.There are thousands of videos like this one on social media, lamenting the "luteal uglies" - the changes in appearance and mood that women say appear during the luteal phase of their menstrual cycle.During this phase, which occurs in the second half of a woman's cycle and ends when she gets her period, women experience a huge drop in oestrogen. So are the "luteal uglies" a real thing?According to Dr Louise Newson, a GP and women's hormones specialist, this change in hormone levels means women can experience a shift in their appearance, sleep and mood during this time. "Our hormones affect our skin, they affect our collagen, so a lot of people find their skin becomes drier, their complexion not so bright, they might have acne and spots," Newson explains. "They might get bloating and breasts can change shape."Elena, who works in hospitality and as an actress in London, says she feels lethargic and "completely unmotivated" during her luteal phase."I feel like my brain is working in slow motion, I tend to become clumsy and way more forgetful," she says. "I don't want to socialise as much and I feel low."Newson says that while women are starting to talk more about the impact of their cycles, many still do not know what to do about it."These women are genuinely suffering and it's affecting their ability to work, function, socialise and just exist," she says.The response to women's concerns can also be frustrating, she adds."Would you say to a man 'Oh your testosterone is down, just don't go to the gym, have a duvet day?' It's unacceptable that women have to put up with it."Your relationships may also change during the luteal phase, Newson says - which is something freelance journalist Henrietta experiences."If I find myself wanting to get irritated with my wonderful, hilarious, chilled out partner there's an extremely high chance I haven't had my coffee, haven't eaten or that I am in my luteal phase," said the 30-year-old.It also affects her friendships. "With my friends, I tend to either overshare and regret it, or isolate myself from them and regret it."More education and discussion about menstrual cycles are needed, says Elena, who only learned about the luteal phase through social media at the age of 24.O'Neill says there is "so little education that women receive about the fundamental aspects of how their bodies work".So much so that many women have turned to TikTok for help. In one video, which has 2.4 million views, a young woman asks: "Ladies, what do you do during your luteal phase to feel better?! I honestly can't cope any more."There are thousands of comments, with one follower suggesting to "wear baggy clothes and avoid the mirror", and another saying "eat chocolate". Another writes that the luteal phase makes her "avoid my husband", while someone else says they cope by watching television "with a bottle of wine".But this advice may actually be detrimental - so what can help women cope with their luteal phase symptoms?Understanding that it's a "predictable, temporary phase" is important, says O'NeillNutrition is key during the luteal phase, she adds - and staying hydrated can help reduce puffinessEasing off salty foods, reducing alcohol intake, and keeping up movement can all help tooSteering clear of processed foods and alcohol will help you avoid increased inflammation, Newson explainsYou should see a health professional if you are particularly struggling during the luteal phase, Newson adds, encouraging women to advocate for themselves"If people don't get what they think is acceptable in the first, second, third, appointment they should go and see someone else. These symptoms don't usually go on their own," she says.

schema.headline: Are the 'luteal uglies' a real thing?

title: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
description: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started
body: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.Spanish officials said the documents of 5%-10% of passengers were being checked before they were allowed to disembark planes. Italy has also said its border controls are random.  The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules.Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ​border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy.Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta.Italy has said that Spanish and EU citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents.However, it is not clear how border officials were meant to distinguish between EU and non-EU travellers and El Pais has reported that several Italian airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks.As for Spanish controls, the authorities insists the immigration checks are random. However, a passenger arriving in Madrid on Saturday told national broadcaster RTVE that all passengers on her flight had had to show their passports. "They told us we couldn't get off the plane without showing our documents," Elisa said. Another passenger said "we were stopped and asked for identification, which the police seemed to approve of".Spain says its checks will stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period". Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia.Italy's decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended.Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. One hundred are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls", still remain there.Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. But BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August, including some that advertised swimming equipment for sale. Six of these groups had more than 100,000 followers. Meta says it has removed posts that violate its policy.The Spanish prime minister's office told El Pais they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week.

schema.headline: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies

title: Gloucestershire woman, 97, breaks record for oldest wingwalker
description: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinnes
body: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinness World Record for being the oldest female wing walker.Betty Bromage, who lives in Cheltenham, broke her own record which was set when she did the same challenge four years ago.Bromage raised funds for the stroke unit at Cheltenham General Hospital – where staff cared for her when she was sick.Speaking about having done six wing walks since the age of 87, she said: "I'd just get bored of life otherwise. I can't drive, I can't see very well and I get a bit frustrated. So, I want to do the things I can do."Image source, Betty BromageImage caption, Betty Bromage says she would be "bored" if she didn't do wingwalksIn August last year, Bromage had a stroke, which still affects her speech."They [the hospital] treated me so well. It affects my words but the rest of me is fine," she said.Image caption, Bromage broke her own record by completing the wingwalkShe added she raises money for charity because it can make a difference - and because she was inspired by some words she read on a hospital wall where she worked as a nurse."It said 'we pass through this world but once, any good we can do, any kindness we can show, do it now, do not defer or neglected, you will not pass this way again'," Bromage said.Image caption, Imogen Sims said it was "amazing" that Bromage was doing the challengeImogen Sims from Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals charity said staff were grateful Bromage is raising money for them."To take on such a daring challenge to support our team is amazing," Sims added."Donations will be used for equipment and will make a real difference for patients and staff."Bromage added: "The only problem is getting up on the wing because I'm quite short. Once you're up there, no problem. The fairground is a lot worse."I'll have to think of something when I'm 100 - something special."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

schema.headline: Gloucestershire woman, 97, breaks record for oldest wingwalker

title: Birmingham Airport baggage issues leave hundreds without luggage
description: She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be load
body: She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane. But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded. "We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said."It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last"."There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said. "It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."Simon Leyland's bags also didn't make it with him to Rome after he travelled on a Jet2 flight from Birmingham on Friday to join a cruise with his family. "We were sat there yesterday with no bags, no record of any bags and the cruise line saying 'our coach is going to set off, and if you don't get on it you won't get on the ship'."There are 30 other people on our cruise in a similar position," Leyland, from Barton-under-Needwood, added. While in Messina, on Sicily, he managed to track his luggage to Rome using AirTags. One of the bags had spent the night at Liverpool's John Lennon Airport, while another had visited Manchester.He is now hopeful the family will be reunited with the luggage in Corfu next week, but said communication about the problem had been "awful"."Things can go wrong, no reasonable person thinks it should always be perfect, but there should be a point where it's like, 'we understand, it's an issue and we'll just over-communicate and we'll tell you where they are'."Clive Stokes, from Kidderminster, who travelled to Cyprus, said delays at the airport were "understandable" given the problems. "But what the airport didn't do is explain the situation to people." He said he had received an email on Friday evening, "two hours into our flight, saying there was a good chance our baggage wouldn't be there".On arrival, only "about 20 cases" had came through, he added. "I've probably spent between three and four hundred euros today on my credit card just to buy stuff, which, I think, I hope they'll reimburse," he added. "It's not the end of the earth, but there were people on the flight who were getting married, so they've got wedding dresses missing."Birmingham Airport said holiday company Jet2 had contacted all affected passengers, and other third parties were also working to reunite passengers with repatriated bags. An airport spokesperson said: "We are continuing to experience an issue with our baggage systems which is impacting some outbound luggage. "Engineers are on site and working to resolve this issue as quickly as possible. Terminal colleagues are also working hard to ensure baggage in terminal is being processed as quickly as possible. "We expect this to cause inconvenience for some passengers, and we sincerely apologise for this. Those due to travel today, should still arrive at the airport in line with Airline advice."TUI has been approached for comment. Some flights from Bristol Airport are being diverted through Birmingham after flights were suspended due to a runway defect.

schema.headline: Birmingham Airport baggage issues leave hundreds without luggage

title: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster
description: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month
body: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month in Wales as part of the Chernobyl Lifeline programByOscar EdwardsBBC WalesUpdated 2 August 2026In the summer of 1999, 11-year-old Anton Honchanka was looking to escape his contaminated hometown following history's worst nuclear disaster.His journey would take him from Gomel, Belarus, to a United Kingdom that was experiencing a historic total solar eclipse, a major political reshuffle by Prime Minister Tony Blair, and a music chart dominated by singles such as Livin' La Vida Loca.Anton was one of the children evacuated from Belarus following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine, after a reactor at the plant exploded and spewed out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Due to radiation, parents in Eastern Europe saw the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline program (CCPL) as vital for their children's health with more than 56,000, external coming to the UK for medical aid and humanitarian support.Thirteen years on since the incident, and with the radiation still hanging in the air, Anton had set off on what he saw then as a "new adventure" thanks to the programme, albeit one "not easy" for his mum to see him leave."My mum was really happy that I had the opportunity to go on the trip," said Anton, now 38."But it wasn't easy for her not having me at home."Anton travelled by bus to Minsk, the capital of Belarus, and from there he flew to the UK.His first clear memory upon arriving in the UK was meeting his first host family. "That's where my experience in Wales really began," he said."My first impression was how peaceful and welcoming everything felt. It had such a cosy atmosphere that I felt comfortable almost straight away."Anton said the architecture was "different" from what he was used to in Belarus, with clean streets and a "warm and cosy atmosphere".His trip came at a time when Belarusian people were living in an increasingly authoritarian state, external, according to the UN Refugee Agency, in a period marked by severe political crackdowns and economic stagnation.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton, centre, stood with Dmitry on his left and the Amoss familyAnton and another boy called Dmitry spent the first two weeks with Angela Davies and her sons. Despite the language barrier, he said they all understood each other "perfectly".They were then taken to Llanharry, Rhondda Cynon Taf, to live with Peter and Linda Amoss.They welcomed the boys into their home with "incredible warmth", said Anton, finding ways to "spoil" and "surprise" them."They often took us shopping because they wanted to treat us," he said."They were always thinking about how they could make us smile."Anton said he naturally became great friends with their kids Gethin and Charlotte spending their time playing outside, riding bikes and enjoying their time together."Those are memories I'll always treasure," he added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton visited landmarks such as St Fagans National Museum of HistoryFor Anton, returning home meant going "back to normal life" and he was surprised to find that "nothing had really changed".He and Dmitry gradually lost touch as they lived in different cities."When we arrived in Minsk, I got on a bus to Gomel, and he wasn't on it," he added.Now with two sons of his own, Honchanka said Wales and its people have "stayed in my heart forever"."I would really love to see my host families again if I have the opportunity.""During that time, they became very close and dear to me."Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton said they became his 'second family' during his time in WalesThis year marked 40 years since the Chernobyl nuclear disaster which caused a reactor to start spewing out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Children from Belarus and Ukraine stayed with host families for four-week recuperative breaks. The clean air, untainted food and clean water helped to lower the levels of caesium and other radiation stored in the children's bodies.Gerrie Bayley, 74, from Prestatyn, first joined the CPPL in 2004 taking in two girls from Belarus.She enjoyed the experience so much, it has since "become her life" and she now serves as the chair of the charity's north Wales branch.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Dmitry, in the Liverpool shirt, lost contact with Anton when they returned to BelarusGerrie said the few weeks in the UK made a remarkable difference to their health."They would sleep all the time. They had these big black circles under their eyes. "By the end of the month, they had energy and were eating well. I cannot say how much difference it made."The communities rallied around the program providing second-hand clothing, free dentist appointments and eye tests for the children."They all had treatment they needed. So many stores helped out." she said.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton became great friends with the Amoss kids during his stayLinda Amoss, 71, said the family were vetted to make sure they had a spare bedroom with enough capacity to house Anton and Dmitry"As far as they were concerned we were a second family."They had already been in the country for a couple of weeks and we were the second family for the latter two weeks of their stay."Linda said she was told that any time spent outside of Belarus would "benefit their health"."There were children with incredibly high rates of cancer in certain areas," she added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton has two sons of his own called Dmitry and DemyanLike Anton, she said the language was something they had to overcome, but it ultimately proved no issue as the boys "just clicked in"."Food was sometimes a bit of an issue, but my cooking isn't the best anyway," she added.Anton joined the family on trips to local landmarks such as St Fagans, Oakwood Theme Park and Garth Hill. "I don't remember them being particularly homesick because everything was sort of just so new and bright for them," said Linda.Image source, Linda AmossImage caption, Peter and Linda Amoss looked after Anton for two weeks during his stay As the four weeks drew to a close, Linda said she understood that the chance of the boys being able to return to the UK was "very slim" due to the demand for places in Ukraine and Belarus.Until now, she had not heard from Anton or Dmitry, but said it would be "extremely brilliant" if they could meet in person again.She also takes great pride in Wales' role in the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline programme."Wales is incredibly hospitable, and I really do love that about our country," she added.

schema.headline: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster

title: Poo, parking and poor pitching - the Lake District's summer battles
description: Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Lake District authorities say litter, fly-camping and irresponsible behaviour are big problems over the s
body: Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Lake District authorities say litter, fly-camping and irresponsible behaviour are big problems over the summer monthsByFederica BedendoNorth East and CumbriaMillions of people visit the Lake District every year, but not all of them abide by the Countryside Code's plea to "leave no trace". It means for enforcement officers and volunteers, summer is often marked by irresponsible parking, inconsiderate camping and even human waste - which doesn't quite have the same ring to it as the Summer of Love."Fifty-plus members of the public engaged with, 10 overnight campers spoken to, eight bags of rubbish collected and they had the joy of seeing one man using a bush as his toilet," reads out Judith Derbyshire, a Westmorland and Furness councillor.It is an extract from a report by patrol officers responsible for tackling anti-social behaviour, who were out in the Coniston area one weekend in July."I'm going to lower the standard of the conversation here but the issue is to do with human poo," says Derbyshire, although she might have used slightly more colourful language.She is responsible for community safety at the Liberal Democrat-led council and says since Covid there has been a surge in visitors who arrive without plans for accommodation, meaning fly-camping is rife.Fly-camping takes place away from designated camp sites and without landowners' permission."Don't feel you can just come up, park up on a lay-by and then go and put a tent up down by the lake shore - you shouldn't be doing that," she says.Image caption, Volunteer litter pickers are often left to deal with the aftermath of fly-campingIt is not just about the litter. Derbyshire says people are also chopping down branches and trees to light fires, causing damage to the environment."There's a tree down at Ullswater, as you're driving down the A592."It's a very large oak tree and somebody fairly recently has put a bonfire up the hollow inside it and, sorry, it's a lovely, big, old oak tree and I want it to be there in a long time to come." Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Problems include people chopping down trees to light firesWestmorland and Furness Council and Cumberland Council are responsible for looking after parts of the Unesco World Heritage Site.Together with Cumbria Police, they can enforce Public Spaces Protection Orders (PSPOs), which help tackle anti-social behaviour.It means in areas covered by a PSPO they have extra powers, such as making someone leave the site or issuing a fine.   Derbyshire says Westmorland and Furness officers have only issued eight tickets so far this summer, as enforcement is seen as a last resort.Instead, the authority tries to "engage, educate and encourage"."If we've perhaps gone out and seen a group in the evening and then gone back in the morning and they're not tidying up, they've done damage and they've said they weren't going to have a bonfire and they obviously have and it's still burning, then that gets to the enforcement stage," she says.Image source, Westmorland and Furness CouncilImage caption, Councillor Judith Derbyshire says officers are often left to deal with the mess from fly-campersEnforcement is made difficult by the fact the council has "very few" officers and there is no round-the-clock response service, Derbyshire says."Putting it bluntly, we are going to have strong cutbacks from our funding as a local authority, we're not going to have the staff to be able to put that sort of thing in place."Fines for breaching a PSPO are currently at £100, but Derbyshire says the government is expected to issue new guidance which could see them raise to £500.For irresponsible parking, councils can issue a £50 ticket which is reduced if paid within a certain timeframe."The problem that we've got now is that a parking ticket is not really a deterrent," says Rob Lewis, a senior manager at Cumberland Council's highways department."If there's four or five people in a vehicle, some of them will just share the cost of that ticket and they'll take it as a parking charge - so it's almost part of the expense of the day out."He says the Labour-led council is in talks with the British Parking Association and other authorities to see if higher charges would be more beneficial in areas such as the Lake District National Park.At busy times, he says, buses have had to be cancelled because badly parked cars are not leaving enough room for them to pass.Image source, Nicola MillnerImage caption, A tent surrounded by litter was left by Windermere last year - one example of the fly-camping the area seesLocal social media pages often show cars parked in front of farm gates, passing places and even private fields.Were there to be a medical emergency or a fire, the stakes would be even higher, Lewis says."We do try and educate the visitors before they come to say where it is appropriate to park and where it isn't appropriate to park."To try and ease congestion on the narrow country roads, shuttle buses serve the most popular areas including Buttermere and the Wasdale Valley, and many operators offer free travel to under-16s during the summer.While Cumberland Council has a team of 25 officers issuing parking tickets, they are spread across the whole authority area, from Millom to Carlisle.Lewis says there is more focus on the Lake District at busy times, but not all bad parking can be enforced by the council."It's not that easy, we cannot issue [tickets] unless there's a restriction in place or unless there's a yellow line down there, or it's part of a disc zone, for example."Image source, Wasdale Action Group/A Wasdale LadImage caption, Social media pages often share images of parking problems in the Lake DistrictHe says problem areas can be flagged to the council, but restrictions may take up to a year to come into force, due to the length of time it takes to go through the process and consult with affected residents.The police have powers to deal with certain issues, such as if a vehicle is causing an obstruction.Derbyshire says people can also contact police if they see anyone behaving in a dangerous way, such as lighting a bonfire that is likely to spread to a large area."We're not encouraging people to go and approach people, but more to feed the information back to us," she says.Image source, Nicola MillnerImage caption, Litter is a blight on beauty spots around the lakesDescriptions of people involved and any vehicle registrations would help them track offenders down, Derbyshire says.She believes working together with residents, visitors and bodies such as the National Trust and other landowners is key to getting the situation under control."We want people to come to Lake District and it's good that there's a wider range of people coming here, it's just that we need to get them educated so they know what they can do and what they can't do."Follow BBC Cumbria on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Cumbria on BBC Sounds. title: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG
description: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second h
body: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second half of Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg drew an appreciative response from senior figures at the club.With much made of United's activity - or lack of - in the transfer market this summer, it was good timing that Tielemans could make his debut when Mason Mount, arguably the club's player of pre-season, needed to be replaced after just 20 minutes.Head coach Michael Carrick told Norwegian broadcaster VG post-match that Mount had come off as a precaution after taking a hefty blow to his foot. The former Chelsea midfielder walked freely past reporters to the team bus an hour after the final whistle.Nevertheless, Tielemans was a surprise signing when Manchester United triggered a previously unknown £35m clause in the Belgian's contract at Aston Villa to agree a five-year deal.There was a lot of debate in the immediate aftermath about how much football the 29-year-old, who made his professional debut for Anderlecht when he was just 16, had played.It obscured his talent.Against PSG he did not do anything particularly special.There were a couple of 45-yard cross-field passes that found their intended targets. There were some simple first-time lay-offs to team-mates within 10 yards.There was also a short sprint just outside the United area to close down dangerman Khvicha Kvaratskhelia when Tielemans recognised the PSG star could be about to take possession within shooting distance.He got there, won the ball and played a simple pass, taking the ball out of harm's way.This isn't really what got the United contingent purring.They were reacting to the little passes between Tielemans and Fernandes, which allowed United to ease their way out of trouble or move up the pitch.Fernandes was the key man last season as United finished third. Nine goals and 21 assists was a decisive contribution in returning the club to the Champions League after a two-year absence.Tielemans showed in his brief cameo he can take some of the pressure off the Portuguese."Youri has consistently been one of the most outstanding midfielders in the Premier League throughout the past seven years," said director of football Jason Wilcox on Tielemans' signing."He will add further composure, creativity and leadership to our squad."He has all of the technical qualities, as well as the ambition and mentality, to thrive at Manchester United."If Wilcox reflects on those words as United head off to the Republic of Ireland for their week-long training camp in Maynooth, he can be quite pleased with himself.It was only 26 minutes, but on that evidence, he has got it spot on.Carrick has confirmed Marcus Rashford will rejoin the Manchester United squad for their trip to the Republic of Ireland.Rashford, England team-mate Kobbie Mainoo and Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez are the final three players to return for United after the World Cup.Although it was not expected Rashford would return to the club when he joined Barcelona on loan in July 2025, the La Liga champions failed to trigger a £26m option to buy the 28-year-old at the end of the season.Despite interest elsewhere, there has been no deal, meaning Rashford will return to United for the first time since January 2025, when he moved to Aston Villa after falling out with former manager Ruben Amorim.United are training at the plush Carton House hotel in Maynooth and have a friendly with Leeds United at Croke Park on 12 August.They complete their pre-season programme against Amorim's new club AC Milan in Wroclaw on 15 August, when Rashford could make his first United appearance since December 2024 if Carrick decides Wednesday is too soon.A former team-mate, coach and manager of Rashford, it has been felt if anyone can patch up the relationship between club and player - which includes his number 10 shirt being given to Matheus Cunha who is also due to be on the trip after a minor injury ruled him out of the Gothenburg encounter - it is Carrick."I've played with him. I played in the game he made his debut, so we have a history," Carrick said."We have got a full squad this week in Dublin. We fly straight there and have a few days where we have the whole group back together. Marcus is part of that, and Kobbie [Mainoo] and Lisandro [Martinez]. We look forward to seeing them."

schema.headline: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG

title: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait
description: Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran war
body: Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reopening of the vital waterway.Both sides suggested on Saturday that discussions were progressing, but a timeline on any deal being finalised remained unclear. Oman's foreign ministry warned against attacks on shipping that could hamper that.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks were in their final stages but the reopening of the strait remained "subject to other conditions".Tehran has effectively blockaded the waterway, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas usually flows, since the US and Israel began attacking it in February.Talks in recent days have focused on the possibility of a deal between Iran and Oman on a new route through the strait, which they would both have responsibility for and is hoped would lead to progress in resuming shipping traffic.But Araghchi said a full reopening of the typically busy maritime route depended on other conditions being met, of which he provided a cursory appraisal.He said the conditions included Iran receiving compensation from the US for what Tehran described as violations of the deal both sides signed in June to cease fighting and advance talks to end the war.That deal - called a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) - quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after it was signed.Separately, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, Iran's security chief, told the semi-official news agency Tasnim that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the US "corrects" its behaviour.He said the US needed to meet six Iranian demands, including a halt to threats against Iran, removal of its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release of Iran's frozen assets.Another blockade, on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, had been imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July.Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran "could be soon", but Vice-President JD Vance appeared to be more sceptical on Saturday, telling Fox News that work remained to be done even if progress was being made."We're really in the middle of the game here," he said. "This thing is not over."Vance added that "we're applying a whole host of tools - diplomatic, economic [and] military tools - to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people".Additionally, he claimed that the "same amount of oil" will emerge from the Gulf as did before the US military operation began on 28 February, although he offered no details."What we're really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships can pass through safely," he added.One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's reported threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Reuters - citing an Iranian official - previously reported that Tehran was seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from vessels who travel through it.Vance downplayed those reports, saying: "The Iranians have told us they have no plans to toll the Strait of Hormuz."Oman's warning against attacks on ships in the strait came as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) said on Saturday that Iran had targeted a tanker affiliated with Adnoc, its state-owned oil company, as it passed through.The UAE's foreign ministry said in a statement that a "hostile Iranian attack" had hit an Adnoc tanker "with a missile". It added that there were no casualties.Later on Saturday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency also reported a ship being struck by "an unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman, causing "a fire that has been extinguished" but no casualties.It is unclear whether UKMTO was referring to the same ship as the UAE.

schema.headline: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait

title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
description: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on t
body: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera."I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time."If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman. "Phone photos have warped our perception of time."It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds."Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since. "Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis, external - the inability to choose because there are so many options.When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that"."Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.Additional reporting by Amy Walker.

schema.headline: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'

title: St Mirren start strongly using relegation scare as 'fuel'
description: Getting back to basics seems key for last seasons' League Cup winners, according to manager Craig McLeish. That and using the negative feeling that pl
body: Getting back to basics seems key for last seasons' League Cup winners, according to manager Craig McLeish. That and using the negative feeling that play-off last season brought as motivation."I'm still using that as fuel," he told BBC Scotland. "I don't want to be involved in that. "We've got a massive journey ahead of us and we have to keep building. Six points out of six is a great start."It helps with the belief in each other. I've said to the boys I have confidence in them. "Last season, we had two horrendous play-off games - even the emotion about it, there were so much nerves when we stepped on the pitch."We have to be horrible to play against. Two clean sheets sets us up well for that. "We want to be really good at the basics and not get bored of that."The running, energy and desire. We want to be fit and strong and relentless this season against whoever we play. We have to keep those standards really high. We did it last week and lived up to it again."It is a sentiment shared by new goalkeeping recruit Jacob Chapman, whose penalty save early in the second half laid the platform before Killian Phillips converted from the spot."Defenders throwing their bodies on the line; [Alex] Gogic throwing his head here and everywhere," he told BBC Scotland."Even the attackers coming back and helping defend."It sets the tempo for the season. It doesn't mean you're going to win every game or even have a great season, but it definitely helps."And it's what a great season looks like at the start. We've started well. "A bit scrappy in some areas and we need to clean that out, but there was still some really nice football getting played in certain areas."McLeish has not hidden from the idea that St Mirren's model is to develop and move players on. The standout example right now is Killian Phillips, the 24-year-old midfielder who has scored all three of their Premiership goals this season and is a big influence on the team as a whole."He's at the stage right now where he's round about the 100-game mark for the club," he said. "He'll be looking for the next step in his career."If he attracts interest, then great. We're doing our job. I'm doing my job."I believe that the longer he stays and plays with me and with us, I'll get him the best move he possibly can."And if that's this window then fine. If it's in January, if we get him to the end of the season, it's part of it and we have to be prepared for any outcome."But we're just delighted to have him as part of our group. He's a massive part of it. And, if he keeps playing like that, his future takes care of itself."
